kurz: How an ETF works both as a pool of fund assets and as an exchange-traded security, and which mechanism in the background ties the market price to the value of the fund.

bloecke.md:
An ETF is two things at once. Without this distinction, you can understand neither the price on the screen nor the spread you pay when buying. On the one hand, an ETF is a fund, that is, a holding of shares whose composition follows an index. On the other hand, it is a security that is traded like a share in the order book of a stock exchange. Between the two sits a mechanism in which no private investor is involved. Only this mechanism ensures that the market price does not drift away from the value of the fund's assets.

## The fund as segregated assets

Legally, many UCITS ETFs launched in Germany are [[Segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)|segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)]]. Segregated fund assets are managed by a fund management company (KVG) but not held in custody by it. For every segregated UCITS fund, Section 68(1) KAGB (German Investment Code) requires an independent depositary to be appointed. The assets are either owned by the company in trust or co-owned by the investors (Section 92(1) KAGB). For the event of insolvency, Section 99(3) KAGB stipulates that the segregated fund assets do not form part of the insolvency estate if insolvency proceedings are opened over the assets of the management company. ETFs from Ireland or Luxembourg are not segregated fund assets within the meaning of the KAGB; they are governed by the law of their home country. For them too, the UCITS Directive requires a depositary, and their fund assets are kept separate from the assets of the management company.

This leads to a point that is regularly misunderstood. The statutory deposit protection of €100,000 per customer and institution is irrelevant to ETF units. It covers balances on the settlement account but not securities. Fund units need no such protection, because they never become part of the assets of the provider or the broker.

Section 206 KAGB limits what the fund may hold with the 5/10/40 rule. At most 5% per issuer is permitted, or up to 10% if the investment conditions provide for it, and all positions above 5% may together make up no more than 40%. Index ETFs fall under the more generous exception in Section 209 KAGB, provided the index is recognised by BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority), sufficiently diversified and appropriately published. They may then invest up to 20% per issuer, and even up to 35% in a single issuer. Without this exception, some country indices could not be replicated at all. Both rules implement Articles 52 and 53 of the UCITS Directive, which funds from Ireland and Luxembourg also follow.

On 8 September 2026, around 2,970 ETFs were listed on Deutsche Börse, plus 205 ETCs and 361 ETNs. ETCs and ETNs look like an ETF in the portfolio but are debt securities of the issuer. A gold ETC is a collateralised bond and not a segregated pool of assets. If the issuer becomes insolvent, everything depends on the collateral, because the insolvency protection for fund assets does not apply here.

## Primary market and the issue of new units

An ETF has no fixed number of units. Units are created and disappear depending on demand, but not through purchases in a savings plan. New units are created exclusively by an [[Authorised participant|authorised participant]]. This is an approved trading bank that has a contract with the fund company for this purpose. The authorised participant delivers the index's basket of shares in the prescribed composition to the company and receives a block of new fund units in return, known as a creation unit. Conversely, it returns units and receives the basket of shares in exchange. These blocks are large; the exact number of units is stated in the prospectus of the fund concerned.

The fact that the exchange is usually made for securities rather than cash affects costs. With a redemption in kind, the fund does not have to sell anything; it passes the shares on directly. The transaction costs of the exit are therefore borne by whoever exits, and not by the investors who remain in the fund. This is where an ETF differs from a traditional retail fund. A retail fund has to sell securities when money flows out and burdens the remaining holdings with the costs.

bloecke.md:
## How the market price is tied to the basket value

Nobody guarantees that an ETF trades at the value of its basket. With ETFs from Ireland or Luxembourg, units bought on the stock exchange usually cannot be returned directly to the fund; that route is used by the authorised participant. If the market price deviates significantly from the net asset value, for example because no market maker is quoting prices any more, the guidelines of the European securities regulator ESMA provide that UCITS ETFs should also allow investors who bought on the stock exchange to redeem units directly. With a German fund held as segregated fund assets, any investor can demand redemption (Section 98 KAGB), less a redemption charge where applicable. The close link in normal operation arises solely because money can be made from a deviation.

If the market price is above the value of the basket, the authorised participant buys the shares on the market, delivers them to the fund, receives new units and sells them at a higher price on the stock exchange. The additional supply pushes the price back down. If the price is below the basket value, it does the reverse. It buys cheap units on the stock exchange, returns them to the fund and sells the basket of shares it receives for them. Both only work as long as the basket itself can be traded.

Assume a block of 50,000 units of a world ETF. The calculated value per unit is €100.00, and the unit trades on the stock exchange at €100.40. That corresponds to a premium of 0.4%.

- Buy the basket of shares for 50,000 units: €5,000,000
- Deliver the basket, receive 50,000 new units and sell them on the stock exchange: €5,020,000
- Assumed transaction and creation costs: €0.05 per unit, so €2,500

This leaves a profit of €17,500. The incentive is so large that a premium of 0.4% on a liquid world ETF does not even arise in normal times. The block size and fees are assumed here; the applicable values are in the prospectus.

bloecke.md: The market price of an ETF does not establish any claim against the fund. It reflects how the market values the basket. It only stays close to the basket value because a deviation would be a profit for the authorised participant. If the underlying securities are barely traded any more, the mechanism remains in place, but it becomes expensive and the gap can widen.

## Three prices of an ETF

For every ETF there are three price figures at the same time, and orders are executed at only one of them. The net asset value is determined once a day after the close of trading and is the basis of the fund's accounting. The [[iNAV]] is the indicative net asset value, which Deutsche Börse or an appointed service provider recalculates every 15 to 60 seconds during trading hours. Market makers use it as the reference for their quotes. Finally, the market price is the price that comes about in the order book.

The iNAV is itself an estimate whose accuracy depends on the time of day. An MSCI World ETF holds around 1,250 stocks, and the US share is around 72% (as of August 2026). Before 15:30 Central European Time, the US stock exchanges are closed, and the US part of the basket is extrapolated. The iNAV is then not wrong, but it is based on a model and not on market prices.

bloecke.md:
## Trading venues

Xetra is the reference system. Continuous trading runs there from 9:00 to 17:30, supplemented by opening, intraday and closing auctions. If a potential price leaves the dynamic or static price corridor, the system interrupts continuous trading for at least 120 seconds (volatility interruption). For ETFs, ETCs and ETNs, a tiered model with widening corridors applies. Xetra has a central order book with several [[Designated sponsor|designated sponsor]] institutions, which are obliged to meet a minimum volume, a maximum spread and a minimum quoting time.

In addition, there are quote-driven trading venues with considerably longer trading hours. Tradegate Exchange and Börse Berlin merged on 1 January 2026 to form the Tradegate Berlin Stock Exchange. On gettex, Baader Bank sets the prices as the sole market maker, and on LS Exchange the firm Lang & Schwarz does so. The longer trading hours are convenient but mean a single price setter instead of an order book. Moreover, the ETF is traded at 7:45 or 22:15, when most of its components are not being traded. In addition, a new rule applies in 2026. Payment for order flow is prohibited under Article 39a MiFIR; the German transition period ended on 30 June 2026. Since then, where a broker routes orders and what this costs have to be reassessed.

bloecke.md:
The first mistake is a market order outside the main trading hours. An unlimited buy order is executed at whatever price the thin order book offers. At 7:45, the market maker quotes small volumes and a wide spread. The surcharge does not appear on any contract note, because it is not a fee.

The second mistake is a stop-loss on a quote-driven trading venue. At night, a single market maker sets the prices there with a wide spread. A brief widening of the spread is enough to turn the stop into a market order, even though nothing has happened on the reference exchange.

It is also wrong to infer narrow spreads from a large fund size. The [[Bid-ask spread|bid-ask spread]] depends on the liquidity of the underlying securities and the number of market makers, not on the size of the fund. Personal finance guides cite three to five basis points for large world ETFs on Xetra. The exchange measures these costs with the Xetra Liquidity Measure (XLM), which states what an immediate purchase and sale of €100,000 costs as a result of the spread and market depth. For the two most actively traded world ETFs, it stood at around 2 basis points in September 2026.

## ETFs in a crash

In March 2020, the structure came under strain across the board for the first time. For equity ETFs, spreads widened for hours to a multiple of their normal level, and volatility interruptions piled up. The deviations were larger for ETFs on corporate bonds. At times they traded at discounts in the single-digit percentage range to their reported net asset value. The lesson does not give exact individual figures, but the order of magnitude is undisputed.

The obvious interpretation that the ETF had not worked was wrong. The net asset value of a bond ETF is calculated from prices that, for many bonds, did not come about at all on that day, because corporate bonds are not traded continuously. The fund value was therefore based on the previous day's prices, while the market price reflected the situation on the current day. In this situation, the ETF price was the more up-to-date information. The discount was the price that buyers demanded for immediate liquidity. Arbitrage continued to work but became expensive, because an authorised participant returning units also has to be able to sell the basket it receives.

An ETF is therefore never more liquid than the securities it contains. With around 1,250 large-cap stocks, this is a theoretical limitation; with two dozen illiquid securities, a very practical one. Moreover, market orders are most expensive in such hours and are placed most often precisely then.

Creation and redemption take place either in kind, that is, in exchange for securities, or in cash, that is, in exchange for money. For broad equity ETFs, the in-kind variant is the norm. The fund exchanges securities for units without trading on the stock exchange itself, and the costs stay with the authorised participant.

Cash settlement occurs when the basket is difficult to obtain, for example with emerging markets that have capital controls, with bonds or with synthetic replication. The fund then trades itself, and part of the transaction costs is incurred in the fund's assets, that is, by all unitholders. These costs do not appear in the TER. They show up in the deviation between the fund return and the index return.

- Always trade with a limit, even with an ETF worth billions. With a market order, you give up control over the price and get nothing in return.
- For world ETFs with a high US share, the time window between 15:30 and 17:30 is suitable. The US stock exchanges are then open, and the iNAV is based on current prices instead of an extrapolation.
- Before placing an order, compare the current iNAV with the bid and ask sides. If there is a conspicuous gap, it is better to wait than to place the order in a hurry.
- Savings plan executions cannot be limited. With monthly contributions, this is an acceptable disadvantage of automation. For a larger lump-sum investment, a manual limit order is the better choice.

mitnehmen: The assets of an ETF are separate from the assets of the management company; with a German fund held as segregated fund assets, they do not form part of the insolvency estate if the company becomes insolvent (Section 99(3) KAGB). The €100,000 deposit protection is neither needed nor applicable here.

Only the authorised participant creates new units, by delivering the basket of shares. Private investors normally trade on the secondary market. With ETFs from Ireland or Luxembourg, they can as a rule only return units directly to the fund if the market price deviates significantly from the net asset value; with a German fund held as segregated fund assets, they can also do so at other times under Section 98 KAGB.
The market price only stays close to the basket value because any deviation would be an arbitrage profit for the authorised participant. This link has an economic basis and is not a legal guarantee.
NAV, iNAV and market price are three different figures. The iNAV is recalculated every 15 to 60 seconds and, for indices with a high US share, is itself an estimate before 15:30.
An ETF is never more liquid than its underlying securities. In March 2020, bond ETFs traded at significant discounts to NAV, and their market price was the more up-to-date price and not a wrong one.

begriffe.text: Assets of an investment fund set up in Germany in contractual form, held separately from the assets of the fund management company. They are held in custody by an independent depositary (Section 68(1) KAGB) and do not form part of the insolvency estate if the company becomes insolvent (Section 99(3) KAGB). ETCs and ETNs are debt securities and therefore not segregated fund assets.

Approved trading bank that, under a contract with the fund company, is the only party allowed to create new ETF units and that returns units to the fund in large blocks. To do so, it delivers the index's basket of shares or receives it on redemption. Through this arbitrage business, it keeps the market price close to the fund value.

Creation and return of ETF units in large blocks (creation units) on the primary market, usually in exchange for securities rather than cash. As a result, the transaction costs are borne by whoever enters or exits and not by the fund's assets.

Indicative net asset value, that is, the value of the fund basket recalculated every 15 to 60 seconds during trading hours. Market makers use it as the reference for their quotes. As long as the underlying securities are not being traded, it is itself an extrapolation.

Market maker approved by the stock exchange that undertakes to quote binding bid and ask prices for a security on a continuous basis. In doing so, it has to comply with a minimum volume, a maximum spread and a minimum quoting time.

Gap between the price at which the market maker buys (bid) and the price at which it sells (ask). It is part of the costs of every order but does not appear on any fee statement. Its size depends on the liquidity of the underlying securities, the number of price setters and the time of day.
